title: Japanese Wisteria: Ancient Wisteria Vines You Can Visit
meta_description: Mostly wild, not trellised: a self-seeded pair near Mount Fuji with National Monument status, and a 1663 shrine vine art historians link to Monet.
intro: Japanese wisteria is usually a garden plant, trained onto a frame and pruned into the tunnels and canopies most visitors picture. The vines mapped here mostly are not. At Yama-jinja, in the shadow of Mount Fuji, two vines seeded themselves and climbed unassisted, one of only eight climbing plants in Japan with National Natural Monument status, granted in 1928; a typhoon later forced the older vine onto a support frame it never asked for. Ichinohe's vine, several hundred years old by local account, is untrained too. Only Tokyo's Kameido Tenjin wisteria followed the cultivated tradition, planted after the shrine's founding in 1663 because the marshy ground suited the species, and it has a claim stranger than its age: art historians trace a line from Hiroshige's 1856 print of it, arched drum bridge and all, to the wisteria Monet later planted at Giverny.
